title: Past Tense: Regular & Irregular
subtitle: The verbs that refuse the -ed.
objectives: Tell regular and irregular past forms apart
Recall the past form of common irregular verbs
Use irregular pasts correctly in writing

cards.title: Some verbs refuse the -ed
cards.text: About two hundred English verbs form their past some other way. They are also the ones you use most.

cards.title: Regular adds -ed. Irregular changes shape
cards.text: There is no rule for the irregular ones. There is only knowing them.
points: **Regular:** *train → trained*, *kick → kicked*.
**Irregular:** *catch → caught*, *build → built*.
**Some do not change at all:** *cut → cut*, *put → put*.
**The common verbs are the irregular ones**, which is bad luck.

cards.title: Tap a verb and watch it change
cards.text: Eight of the ones that matter, each in a sentence. Two quiz questions come from here.

question.text: What is the past tense of 'catch'?
question.explain: Irregular. 'Catched' is the natural guess and it is not a word.

cards.title: Game writing is full of these
cards.text: Quest logs and item descriptions lean on irregular verbs constantly.
points: **I built the base.** Not builded.
**The boss caught me mid-dodge.** Not catched.
**I lost the run on the last floor.** Not losed.
**You already say these correctly** in speech.

question.text: Write the past tense of 'build'. One word.

cards.title: The mistake is logical, which is why it happens
cards.text: Adding -ed to an irregular verb is a sign you understood the rule and applied it too widely.
points: **'He teached me'** — you know -ed makes a past. The verb just refuses.
**Small children do this constantly**, and so do confident learners.
**It is not carelessness.** It is over-applying a good rule.
**Only exposure fixes it.** Read and notice.

cards.title: A race report is irregular verbs end to end
cards.text: Almost nothing in a report about a race takes -ed.
points: **He drove** the last lap on worn tyres. Not drived.
**The engine held** together. Not holded.
**She took** the lead at turn three. Not taked.
**They lost** the podium in the pits. Not losed.

cards.title: Literature Review: Don Quixote, Chapter 12: The Adventure with the Prisoners
cards.text: Quixote meets a line of chained men being marched to the galleys, and decides nobody should be forced anywhere.
points: **He freed them**, against Sancho's advice.
**They thanked him**, then stoned him and ran.
**He had not asked** what any of them had done.
**Freed, thanked, stoned, ran.** Four irregular pasts in one chapter.

options: The blades spun for ten seconds.
The blades spinned for ten seconds.
The blades spined for ten seconds.
question.explain: Spin is irregular: spun. 'Spinned' is the over-regularised guess.

terms.def: Forms its past by changing shape, or not at all.
Adding -ed to a verb that does not take it.
The plain verb, before any ending.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Regular verbs add -ed. Irregular ones change shape.
The most common verbs are the irregular ones.
'Catched' and 'builded' come from applying a good rule too widely.
There is no shortcut. Exposure is the method.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 2 English. The lesson's real work is naming over-regularisation and treating it as a sign of understanding rather than carelessness, because 'catched' and 'builded' come from applying the -ed rule faithfully to verbs that reject it. Saying that out loud removes the embarrassment and makes the fix — exposure — feel reasonable. The interactive carries eight high-frequency irregulars in sentences drawn from boxing, weather, building, a teardown and a race, so the forms arrive attached to contexts rather than as a list.
discussion: Why do people say 'builded' when they know the past tense?
Which verbs do not change at all?
Why are the commonest verbs the irregular ones?
extension: Read a page aloud and mark every irregular past you find.
Write a race report using five irregular verbs.
misconceptions: That a rule exists for irregular forms.
